description: Hey there, join our team and let's blast off!
summary:
We built Orbital Acre to help farmers in Iowa work out what to grow next on their field.
Most farms there just switch between corn and soybean every year. The problem is the soil ends up bare for about half the year, so heavy rain washes it away and takes nitrate with it. A longer rotation could fix a lot of that, but changing what you grow is a big risk when it’s your field and your income.
So we made it simple. You click your field on the map, answer a few quick questions about your farm and what you care about, and the app tests every realistic rotation against over 40 years of NASA weather on your actual soil. You get the best options, what the field looks like month by month, how each one would’ve done in a bad year like the 2012 drought, and the downsides too, like when a rotation makes less money.
It runs on NASA POWER, SRTM and SMAP data alongside USDA and Iowa State research, and we checked our model against NASA’s own soil moisture data and real sensors in the ground. It supports the farmers judgement rather than replacing it, we want farmers to see the evidence for their own field before they bet a season on it.
details:
All code can be found in GitHub repository: Adamfisher-dev/Farm-Adaptation-NASA

What it does

Orbital Acre helps an Iowa farmer compare crop rotations for one field. You click your field on a map, answer a few quick questions about your farm (livestock, buyers, equipment) and set what matters most to you: drought, soil, water quality, income, and pests and fertiliser. About a minute later you see what you grow now next to the best fit for your field and two other options.

How it works

  1. Field lookup. The app pulls the field’s soil from the USDA soil survey (SSURGO), its slope from NASA SRTM elevation, and its crop history from the USDA Cropland Data Layer.
  2. Weather. It takes daily NASA POWER weather for that location from 1984 to 2025.
  3. Crop water use. For every rotation, it works out how much water each crop needs each day using the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith method.
  4. Soil-water balance. It runs a daily soil-water model through all 42 years. That gives drought stress, drainage and bare-soil days for each rotation in each year.
  5. Research-based scores. Things we can’t simulate, like nitrogen from legumes and pest breaks, are scored from published research, mainly Iowa State’s Marsden Farm trial.
  6. Ranking. Each rotation is scored against the farmer’s priorities and compared with their current rotation across many runs with different weather years, prices and weightings. It is also tested in six climates, up to 2 °C warmer with 20% less summer rain.

For each option the farmer gets a month-by-month field calendar, a replay of a hard year like 2012, the benefits, the risks and what to check locally, plus a PDF report to take away.

An example

For a corn–soybean field near Nevada, Iowa, the best fit was a four-year rotation of corn, soybean, oats and alfalfa with a rye cover crop. It beat the current rotation in 99% of runs and stayed the top choice in all six climates. Heavy-rain days on bare soil fell from 6 a year to under 1, and water draining out of the field fell from 299 mm to 179 mm a year. It also earned about $50 an acre less, and the app shows that just as clearly.

Benefits and intended impact

A farmer can test a change on their own field before risking a season on it. Agronomists get a clear starting point for the conversation. If more fields keep something growing through winter and spring, that means less erosion and less nitrate reaching rivers. The tool backs up the farmer’s and agronomist’s judgement. It doesn’t replace it, and it doesn’t predict yield or profit.

Tools

  • Language and app: Python, with Streamlit, hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud
  • Data handling: pandas, numpy, xarray
  • Maps and satellite files: geopandas, shapely, rioxarray, rasterstats, folium
  • Stats and charts: scipy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, matplotlib
  • Data access and testing: requests, earthaccess, pytest
  • NASA data: POWER (daily weather), SRTM (elevation), SMAP (soil moisture, used to check the model)
  • Other data: USDA SSURGO and Cropland Data Layer, FAO-56 crop tables, Iowa State crop budgets, the Marsden Farm rotation trial
  • AI: we used Claude (Anthropic) to plan, draft code and debug, and we reviewed all of it

How it’s creative

It doesn’t just recommend a “best crop”. It runs every rotation through four decades of real weather, so the trade-offs come out of the physics. A rye cover crop protects the soil but uses up spring water, for example, and the app shows both sides. The hard-year replay and the field calendar turn all of that into something a farmer can read at a glance.

What we considered

  • Honesty about scale. The weather is a roughly 50 km grid square, not one field, and soil wetness is modelled, not measured.
  • Trust. Our water calculation matches the FAO-56 worked example (3.88 against 3.9 mm/day), and every run checks that no water is gained or lost. We also checked the model against NASA’s own root-zone soil moisture (match of 0.71), a buried Iowa State probe (0.68) and the Ames weather station (0.97), where 1.00 is a perfect match.
  • Practicality. Options a farm can’t run, like hay without a buyer, are left out, and the app says why.
  • Evidence limits. The Marsden Farm results come from whole systems that also got manure, so we say so.
  • Showing the downsides. If a rotation earns less or struggles in a drought, the farmer sees it.
